condition.label: fibromyalgia
condition.distinctions: Nociplastic widespread pain syndrome; does not label all widespread pain or override coexisting inflammatory/structural diagnoses.

scope.population: Adults with established fibromyalgia; primary strength trial women20–65 and tai-chi trial predominantly middle-aged women.
scope.stage: Chronic symptoms; not acute injury or surgery rehabilitation.
scope.operativeStatus: Primarily nonoperative exercise research; surgical protocols and postoperative clearance not established.
scope.exclusions: Primary studies excluded important participation-limiting comorbidity and competing pain causes; these are applicability limits,not universal exercise bans.
scope.uncertainty: Response and tolerability vary; stretching alone cannot inherit benefit of strength,aerobic or mind-body bundles.

sources.title: Resistance exercise improves muscle strength, health status and pain intensity in fibromyalgia—a randomized controlled trial

access.details: Complete EuropePMC XML PMC4489359 retrieved; eligibility,person-centered intervention,Box1,Tables3/4 and pain-related withdrawals inspected.

integrity.method: Inspected primary article metadata/version and linked notices; Crossref DOI works metadata request and focused later-evidence searches on 2026-11-01. Not a registry-wide clearance.
integrity.result: Crossref lookup returned HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests; no complete external registry check. No notice identified in the retrieved article text; absence not established.

sources.population: Women20–65 meeting ACR1990 criteria;actual22–64,variable chronic symptom duration; competing severe pain/comorbidity excluded.
sources.comparator: Physiotherapist-guided relaxation/autogenic training twice weekly15weeks,followed by stretching.
sources.coInterventions: Person-centered introductory dialogue/group support;strength arm included warm-up and stretching,so not isolated resistance component.
sources.outcomes: Knee-extension force between-group p=0.010,effect size0.55;FIQ p=0.038,effect size0.41;pain p=0.033,effect size0.46. No95%CI for these standardized effects in extracted table. Handgrip/SF36 group differences not significant;13–18month self-report group differences absent.
sources.uncertainty: Unblinded participants,multiple outcomes,attrition;higher-function participants more often reached80%1RM; no durable group benefit established.
sources.harms: Five participants discontinued resistance because increased pain;two still attended post-test. Meanattendance71%strength,64%relaxation.
sources.limitations: Individual readiness governs progression: 42/67 participants (62.7%) reached 80% estimated 1RM. No automatic progression or universal tolerability follows.

protocol.execution: Machine leg press,knee extension/flexion;free-weight biceps/grip;bodyweight heel raise/core stability;10minwarm-up,50minprotocol and10minstretching. Exact machines/core/stretch positions incompletely specified.
protocol.supervision: Experienced physiotherapists,groups5–7 with individual introductory/load-adjustment meeting.
protocol.progression: Evaluate every3–4weeks in patient–therapist dialogue;retain load if participant not ready. Rapid heel raises addedweek5,explosive knee extensionsweek8 within supervised program.
protocol.stoppingRules: Avoid increased pain via modification/person-centered control;no universal numeric stopping threshold reported.

sources.population: Age≥21,ACR1990/2010criteria;92%women,mean52;serious participation-limiting disease,inflammatory/connective-tissue disease and recent tai chi excluded.
sources.comparator: 24weekmoderate aerobic classes twice weekly versus tai chi1or2times/week,12or24weeks.
sources.coInterventions: Routine drugs/physician care permitted;home practice encouraged;warm-up/stretching/breathing/relaxation differ by program.
sources.outcomes: 24weekFIQR combined tai-chi advantage5.5points (95%CI0.6–10.4),below borrowed8.1pointFIQclinical threshold;matched24week2×/weekcontrast16.2 (8.7–23.6). At52weeks combined difference2.7 (−2.3 to7.7),not significant. Twice-versus-once weekly advantage not significant.
sources.uncertainty: Tai-chi attendance62%versus aerobic40%;unblinded participants,complex bundle,unequal adherence and multiple contrasts.
sources.harms: No intervention-related serious adverse events;12events considered related,8tai chi/4aerobic,mostly minor musculoskeletal.
sources.limitations: Tai chi is not a single stretch or strength-set substitute;exact Yang forms not fully extracted for app artwork.

protocol.execution: Classic Yang-style tai chi combines meditative movement,breathing,relaxation; aerobic arm choreographed group cardiovascular exercise plus warm-up/cool-down/stretching.
protocol.supervision: Trained instructors;videos monitored tai chi fidelity;exercise-physiology oversight and technique/HR/RPE monitoring for aerobic.
protocol.progression: Aerobic duration +5min every2weeks,individually tailored. Tai chi weekly practice assignments.
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as one numeric stopping rule;adverse events systematically assessed by rheumatologist.

locations: Methods > Setting and participants; Interventions > Tai chi; Aerobic exercise

access.details: Complete publisher HTML retrieved;methodology,exercise modality recommendations and strength/flexibility evidence/limits inspected.

integrity.method: Inspected primary article metadata/version and linked notices; Crossref DOI works metadata request and focused later-evidence searches on 2026-11-01. Not a registry-wide clearance.
integrity.result: Inspected Crossref metadata has no update-to entry; this does not establish absence of corrections or retractions. No replacement established by focused currentness search.

sources.design: Society evidence-based treatment guideline plus consensus,not one trial.
sources.population: Fibromyalgia management; evidence predominantly women with heterogeneous trials.
sources.comparator: Exercise versus no intervention or active modalities in reviewed syntheses.
sources.outcomes: Recommends aerobic/resistance approaches;flexibility generally less effective and lacks clinically significant advantage versus aerobic for several outcomes.
sources.uncertainty: No universally superior aerobic modality;methodological quality and protocol standardization vary.
sources.harms: Tolerability summaries cannot erase individual pain withdrawals in primary trials.
sources.limitations: No condition-wide high-intensity/ROM ban and no single validated default dose.

protocol.execution: Multiple aerobic,resistance and flexibility approaches;not one precise execution.
protocol.dose: Heterogeneous reviewed protocols;no single optimal dose.
protocol.frequency: Varied protocols;not a common universal frequency.
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as a validated numeric stopping rule.
